summary:
Caribbean Netherlands comprises Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law on civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination extends to the islands, and the statutory framework operating in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form.

That protection covers visitors as well as residents. Travel-facing coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 ranks Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, on the stated basis that as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are covered by strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed.

Same-sex unions have been registrable since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba recorded the Caribbean Netherlands' first: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on the island; both were visiting, which establishes a local record of performing same-sex unions for people who are only passing through.

Ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. The official weddings page of Saba Tourism identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony and documents registrar Julieta Woods as flexible with couples' wishes, alongside a full destination-wedding supply chain of caterers, florists and accommodation.
tangentialFactors:
The equality-friendly positioning described above is travel-facing: the ranking and the welcome it reports come from a destinations list aimed at couples choosing where to marry, not from an assessment of trans-specific conditions. Its regional framing places the islands among the small number of Caribbean and Latin American destinations ranked for marriage equality, which signals how exceptional the Dutch statutory position is in that subregion rather than describing local practice.

Marriage infrastructure is a sustained feature of the islands' offering rather than an occasional accommodation. Saba's tourism body markets full destination-wedding services, which indicates routine registrar capacity and predictable scheduling for a couple planning a ceremony.

The GayCities entry also notes that Bonaire uses the US dollar, a routine currency matter with no bearing on legal status.
localsOnly:
The Census Office in Saba is the body that enters same-sex unions into the register, and it has done so since 4 December 2012. Residency is not a precondition for registration: the first union recorded was between two non-resident visitors, and the registry's practice is to process such applications through the normal civil-ceremony route.

Registrar Julieta Woods is named on Saba's official weddings page as handling civil ceremonies in the Court Room in the Administrative Building and as flexible with couples' wishes, so residents and long-stay couples deal with a single named official for the ceremony itself. Catering, floral and accommodation suppliers on the island work to a documented destination-wedding format.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents for Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba, nor whether a trans visitor's documents are accepted as presented at check-in or at the border.

Entry and screening practice is likewise unsourced: there is no material on what occurs if a traveller's presentation does not match their documents, or whether screening procedures risk disclosing a trans person's status.

Access to gender-affirming care on the islands, including availability of hormones or surgeon referrals and the position on carrying related medication, is not documented here and remains unresolved.

Facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors specifically are not covered by any source; the anti-discrimination protection described in this record rests on Dutch national provisions extending to the islands, and no trans-specific legal text, complaint record or enforcement outcome has been sourced for the territory. The treatment of trans people within the marriage provisions, including whether a partner's gender history affects registration, is also unaddressed.
